strengths: Addresses an important practical bottleneck for multimodal LLM inference: reducing visual-token computation and KV-cache cost while preserving downstream performance.
The proposed ZipR1 formulation is simple and intuitive, combining task accuracy and token reduction in an RL-style post-training objective that is aligned with sparse-attention inference.
Experiments cover three Qwen VL models and 13 image/video benchmarks, with reported token ratios around 21-24% and mostly small accuracy changes relative to full attention.
The paper is generally readable, and the high-level pipeline is easy to understand.
weaknesses: The main acceleration claim is not directly validated. The paper reports token ratio but no wall-clock latency, throughput, memory/KV-cache usage, hardware setup, batch size, or sparse-kernel overhead, so the practical efficiency benefit remains unproven.

Baselines are insufficient. ZipVL is compared at much higher token ratios, but there is no matched-ratio or matched-accuracy comparison against simply lowering ZipVL's threshold, tuning p, or using other token pruning/sparse attention methods.

The evaluation lacks key ablations: no isolation of the accuracy reward, efficiency reward, KL term, random p sampling, group size, training data size, or reference model choice. This makes it hard to attribute the reported gains to the proposed RL method.

Reproducibility is weak. Important training details are missing, including optimization hyperparameters, number of updates, LoRA/full fine-tuning choice, compute budget, data filtering/splits, reward implementation for open-ended answers, and exact evaluation settings.

The mathematical formulation of sparse attention is not fully sound or clear. Masking Q and K by zeros before softmax is not equivalent to selecting a subset of tokens and does not itself reduce computation; the token-budget definition also appears inconsistent with the reported 0-100% ratios.
Reported performance differences are often very small and no variance, confidence intervals, or repeated-run results are provided, making it difficult to judge whether the changes are meaningful.

Novelty is moderate: the method appears to be a straightforward combination of an existing sparse attention method with GRPO and a token-ratio reward, without deeper analysis or strong evidence that RL is necessary.
